title: Short Stuff: The Story of Spirit Halloween
summary: Short Stuff episode on Spirit Halloween, the seasonal pop-up Halloween store chain in the United States. Josh and Chuck cover its origins in the early 1980s with Joe Marver, who started with a women's discount apparel store (Just Spirit Women's Discount Apparel) and pivoted to Halloween merchandise after seeing a costume shop do well across the street. They discuss its growth to around 60 pop-ups by the late 1990s, its 1999 sale to Spencer's Gifts, the Spencer's connection (Spirit Halloween earned about half of Spencer's yearly earnings in 2013), its seasonal operations (roughly August to November 2, with most business in late October), temporary staffing, real estate expansion, and its Spirit of Children charity supporting children's hospitals. The hosts also touch on pop-up retail in general, with a Strong Towns reference on the community benefits of temporary shops.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to Spirit Halloween
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic: Spirit Halloween, a US seasonal Halloween pop-up store chain that appears in abandoned malls and vacant big box stores.

segments.title: Spirit Halloween as a meme and store count
segments.summary: Chuck says the chain has roughly 1,400 to 1,500 seasonal stores and is a Halloween meme, with banners placed on landmarks. He notes Metro Atlanta had 21 locations that year.

segments.title: Pop-up stores and the Strong Towns perspective
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the long North American tradition of temporary pop-up businesses such as Christmas tree lots and flea markets. Josh reads a Strong Towns passage praising temporary shops for entrepreneurs and empty spaces.

segments.title: Joe Marver's origins in women's apparel and the Halloween pivot
segments.summary: Joe Marver founded the chain in the early 1980s. He started with Just Spirit Women's Discount Apparel, then noticed a Halloween costume shop across the street doing well and switched to Halloween merchandise. After a strong first October, he leased a temporary space the next year and sold about $100,000 of Halloween goods in 30 days.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief transition before the hosts return from the break.

segments.title: Growth to about 60 stores and expansion strategy
segments.summary: By the late 1990s the chain had grown to about 60 pop-ups, with the name Spirit Halloween. Growth strategy included billboards, ads, large storefronts near anchor stores, and expanding beyond costumes into decorations and other Halloween goods.

segments.title: Sale to Spencer's Gifts in 1999
segments.summary: Joe Marver sold Spirit Halloween to Spencer's Gifts in 1999 after a trade show meeting in Manhattan. Chuck recalls Spencer's as a 1980s mall store. In 2013, Spirit Halloween contributed about half of Spencer's yearly earnings, which were about $250 million.

segments.title: Seasonal operations, staffing, and real estate
segments.summary: Spirit Halloween operates from about August to November 2, with most sales in the last two weeks of October. It hires around 25,000 temporary workers and plans leases and district managers year-round. The hosts mention senior director of real estate Frank Pasera and a Slate article written by a former district manager.

segments.title: Inventory and costume trends
segments.summary: Josh notes that 30 to 40 percent of inventory carries over each year, and mentions costume sales swings. Chuck asks about Halloween costume plans.

segments.title: Spirit of Children charity
segments.summary: Spirit Halloween supports children's hospitals through its Spirit of Children program. About 150 hospitals receive care packages of costumes and decorations, and the program funds equipment and other support year-round. Donations are accepted in stores and online, with 100 percent going to the program.

segments.title: Closing banter and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts joke about sponsorship and close the Short Stuff episode.
